hints: Read transformation W on the diagram as $\text{Ca(s) + Cl}_{2}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(g) + 2Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$. List the separate steps needed to atomise, ionise and form the anions.
Remember to use two moles of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and to take 1st + 2nd ionisation energies of calcium plus bond energy of $\text{Cl}_{2}$ from the Data Booklet.
walkthrough:
Picture what W really does**
You start at $\text{Ca(s) + Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}$ and finish at $\text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(g) + 2Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$. So you must turn solid calcium into gaseous atoms, turn chlorine molecules into atoms, strip two electrons from calcium and add electrons to two chlorine atoms.

Add the five enthalpy terms**
$$\Delta H_{W} = \Delta H_{at}[\text{Ca(s)}] + D[\text{Cl-Cl}] + IE_{1}[\text{Ca}] + IE_{2}[\text{Ca}] + 2EA[\text{Cl(g)}]$$
$$ = (+193) + (+242) + (+590) + (+1150) + 2(-349) = +1477 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The electron affinity is exothermic so it is negative, but all the atomisation, bond breaking and ionisation steps are endothermic.

hints: Apply Hess law around the outer cycle: going from $\text{Ca(s) + Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}$ up via W then down via Z must equal going via formation of $\text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(s)}$ then solution Y.
Rearrange to $\text{Z = formation + solution - W}$ and watch the signs of the given $-795$ and $-83$ values.
walkthrough:
Link the two routes to aqueous solution**
One route is direct: ions to $\text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(aq)}$, that is Z. The other route is backwards up W, then forwards through formation X and solution Y. By Hess law the total enthalpy change must be the same.

Substitute and calculate**
Going from $\text{Ca(s) + Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}$ to $\text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(aq)}$ via solid is:
$$\Delta H_{f} + \Delta H_{sol} = -795 + (-83) = -878 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
But this also equals $W + Z$, so:
$$Z = (\Delta H_{f} + \Delta H_{sol}) - W = -795 - 83 - 1477 = -2355 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Final answer: $\Delta H_{Z} = -795 - 83 - 1477 = -2355 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recognise Z as the sum of the hydration enthalpies of the separate gaseous ions: $\text{Z} = \Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Ca}^{2+}] + 2\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Cl}^{-}]$.
Rearrange to isolate $\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Ca}^{2+}]$ and substitute $\text{Z} = -2355$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Cl}^{-}] = -364 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Split Z into ion hydrations**
Z takes $\text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(g) + 2Cl}^{-}\text{(g)}$ to the hydrated ions in $\text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(aq)}$. So:
$$Z = \Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Ca}^{2+}] + 2\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Cl}^{-}]$$

Solve for calcium**
$$\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = Z - 2\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Cl}^{-}]$$
$$ = -2355 - 2(-364) = -2355 + 728 = -1627 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The very large negative value reflects the high charge density of the small $2+$ ion.
Final answer: $\Delta H_{hyd}[\text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(g)}] = -2355 - 2(-364) = -1627 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall lattice energy is $\text{Ca}^{2+}\text{(g) + 2Cl}^{-}\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(s)}$. Find two arrows on the diagram that connect those same two levels.
walkthrough:
Match levels to the definition**
Lattice formation goes from the top level (gaseous ions) to the $\text{CaCl}_{2}\text{(s)}$ level. You can go directly down Z to aqueous then back up Y, giving $\text{Z - Y}$. Equivalently you can go back down W to elements then forward down X, giving $\text{X - W}$.
Final answer: lattice energy $= \text{Z - Y}$ or $\text{X - W}$

hints: Compare the sizes of the ions: $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ versus $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ versus $\text{F}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Use size to judge attraction strength**
Lattice energy depends on charge divided by the sum of ionic radii. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{F}^{-}$ is smaller than $\text{Cl}^{-}$. Smaller ions pack closer, so the attraction between $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{F}^{-}$ is stronger and releases more energy. Hence $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ is less exothermic.
Final answer: Less exothermic, because both ions in $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ are larger than those in $\text{MgF}_{2}$ so electrostatic attraction is weaker.

hints: To make $\text{BaSO}_{4}$ by mixing, you need one solution to supply $\text{Ba}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$ and the other to supply $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}\text{(aq)}$, both from soluble sources.
walkthrough:
Choose spectator ion partners that stay in solution**
For example: $\text{BaCl}_{2}\text{(aq) + Na}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_{4}\text{(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}$. Any soluble barium compound plus any soluble sulfate works because only $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ precipitate.
Final answer: A soluble barium salt e.g. barium chloride or barium nitrate, and a soluble sulfate e.g. sodium sulfate or sulfuric acid.

hints: State the observed solubility trend for Group 2 sulfates from magnesium to barium.
Recall $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{lat} + \Sigma \Delta H_{hyd}$ and consider how $\Delta H_{lat}$ changes as the cation gets larger with a large anion.
Consider how $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of the cation changes down the group and why it falls faster than $\Delta H_{lat}$ when the anion is large.
Link the resulting change in $\Delta H_{sol}$ to less favourable dissolving.
walkthrough:
State the trend**
Magnesium sulfate is very soluble, barium sulfate is essentially insoluble. Solubility decreases down Group 2.

Track both energy terms**
As $\text{M}^{2+}$ gets larger, charge density falls. So the lattice with $\text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ is less strongly held and $\Delta H_{lat}$ becomes less exothermic. Similarly, the ion attracts water less strongly so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of the cation also becomes less exothermic.

Decide which dominates for a large anion**
With the large sulfate ion, the relative change in lattice energy down the group is small, because the anion size already dominates the interionic distance. The hydration energy of the small to large cation changes much more. So $\Delta H_{hyd}$ falls faster.

Connect to solution enthalpy**
Since $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{lat} + \Sigma \Delta H_{hyd}$$, the faster loss of exothermic hydration makes $\Delta H_{sol}$ less exothermic or more endothermic down the group. A more endothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$ makes solution less favourable, so solubility falls.

Final answer: Solubility decreases down Group 2.
Both $\Delta H_{lat}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic down the group.
$\Delta H_{hyd}$ decreases more rapidly and is the dominant factor.
Hence $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes less exothermic or more endothermic, so dissolving is less favourable.
